summary.short: Texas SB 1188 adds Health and Safety Code Chapter 183 on electronic health records. It requires U.S. storage, limits access and amendments, mandates record fields including biological sex, gives minors' parents access, permits practitioners' AI diagnostic use with disclosure, and sets agency and attorney general enforcement, effective September 1, 2025.
summary.long: SB 1188 adds Chapter 183 to the Texas Health and Safety Code. Section 183.001 defines terms, including covered entity, which includes health care practitioners but excludes listed facilities and waiver providers. Section 183.002 requires covered entities to keep electronic health records physically in the United States or a U.S. territory, limits access to staff with employment-related need, and requires reasonable safeguards. Section 183.003 requires records to include an option to record metabolic health and diet communications between covered entities. Section 183.004 bars collecting, storing or sharing credit score or voter registration status in records. Section 183.005 permits practitioners to use AI for diagnostic purposes under listed conditions, including review of AI-created records, and requires disclosure of that use to patients. Section 183.006 requires systems for minors' records to allow parents or guardians complete access, subject to legal restrictions. Section 183.007 requires a separate space recording biological sex and sexual development disorders, and requires decision tools to use the recorded biological sex. Section 183.008 limits amendments to biological sex. Sections 183.009 and 183.010 require investigations and allow disciplinary action after three or more violations. Section 183.011 allows attorney general injunctions and civil penalties of up to $5,000, $25,000 or $250,000 depending on culpability. Section 183.012 requires an memorandum of understanding and rules. Section 2 applies the chapter to records prepared on or after the effective date, and the storage rule to storage from January 1, 2026. Section 4 sets the effective date as September 1, 2025.

notes: Effective date conflict: Sec. 2(a) applies Chapter 183 only to records prepared on or after the effective date, while Sec. 2(b) applies Sec. 183.002 to storage on or after January 1, 2026 regardless of when the record was prepared; Sec. 4 sets the effective date as September 1, 2025. Undefined terms: 'the commission', 'appropriate regulatory agency', 'open data' (183.002(b)), 'protected health information' (183.011(b)(3)), and 'covered entity' is defined only by reference to Section 181.001. Sec. 183.001(2) also excludes facilities under Health and Safety Code Chapters 142, 242, 246, 247 and 252 and a waiver provider; only the Human Resources Code Chapter 103 reference is coded as a relation. Section 183.008 and 183.007 concern biological sex entries and are not coded as thresholds.

obligations.summary: Covered entity shall ensure electronic health records under its control that contain patient information are physically maintained in the United States or a U.S. territory, including records stored by third-party, subcontracted or cloud providers.
obligations.applies_from: Storage on or after January 1, 2026 (Sec. 2(b)); otherwise the Act's effective date of September 1, 2025 (Sec. 4) for records prepared on or after that date (Sec. 2(a))

evidence.quote: A covered entity shall ensure that electronic health records under the control of the entity that contain patient information are physically maintained in the United States or a territory of the United States.

obligations.summary: Covered entity shall restrict access to state residents' electronic health record information (other than open data) to individuals who need it for treatment, payment or health care operations, and shall implement reasonable and appropriate administrative, physical and technical safeguards for confidentiality, integrity and availability.
obligations.applies_from: Storage on or after January 1, 2026 (Sec. 2(b)); otherwise the Act's effective date of September 1, 2025 (Sec. 4) for records prepared on or after that date (Sec. 2(a))

evidence.quote: Each covered entity shall implement reasonable and appropriate administrative, physical, and technical safeguards

obligations.summary: Covered entity shall ensure each electronic health record includes the option for a health care practitioner to collect and record inter-entity communications on the individual's metabolic health and diet in treating a chronic disease or illness.
obligations.applies_from: September 1, 2025 for electronic health records prepared on or after that date (Sec. 2(a), Sec. 4)

evidence.quote: A covered entity shall ensure each electronic health record maintained for an individual includes the option for a health care practitioner to collect and record communications between two or more covered entities

obligations.summary: Covered entity may not collect, store or share information on an individual's credit score or voter registration status in the individual's electronic health record.
obligations.applies_from: September 1, 2025 for electronic health records prepared on or after that date (Sec. 2(a), Sec. 4)

evidence.quote: A covered entity may not collect, store, or share any information regarding an individual's credit score or voter registration status in the individual's electronic health record.

obligations.summary: A health care practitioner using artificial intelligence for diagnostic purposes must act within the scope of the practitioner's license, must not use it where otherwise restricted or prohibited by state or federal law, and must review all AI-created records consistent with Texas Medical Board medical records standards.

enforcement.max_penalty_text: $5,000 per violation committed negligently in a single year; $25,000 per violation committed knowingly or intentionally in a single year; $250,000 per violation in which the covered entity knowingly or intentionally used protected health information for financial gain
enforcement.penalty_formula: Tiered per-violation maxima: $5,000 (negligent, single year); $25,000 (knowing or intentional, single year); $250,000 (knowing or intentional use of protected health information for financial gain). Continuing violations within a year are counted once per violation regardless of duration.
